findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Performance Report Mid Suffolk
findings.headline: Customer service call performance degraded significantly; abandonment rate at 30% vs 10% target
findings.detail: Call answer times doubled to 318 seconds (target 105) and call abandonment rates tripled to 30% (target 10%), with June seeing a 40% spike in call volumes compared to June 2025. The council attributes this to the Simpler Recycling service rollout on 1 June and concurrent staff vacancies. Stage 1 complaints increased to 323 from 287 in Q4, with the increase attributed to recycling service transitions.
findings.matters: A 40% call spike and 30% abandonment rate indicates service capacity is inadequate for operational demands, raising questions about the adequacy of staffing levels and the financial impact of the recycling transition.
findings.figures: 318 seconds (actual) vs 105 seconds (target); 30% abandonment vs 10% target; 4,276 additional calls in June 2025 vs June 2026; 323 complaints (Q1) vs 287 (Q4)
findings.quote: Better recycling and staff vacancies have impacted on call handling performance. In June better recycling was implemented throughout the districts and as a result call volumes and overall contact spiked for a second month in a row. Compared to June 2025, the team received an additional 4276 calls, an increase of 40%.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Performance Report Mid Suffolk
findings.headline: HRA void relet times 40% over target, flagged as a key priority concern
findings.detail: Average relet time reached 84.13 days against a 60-day target, up from 80.75 days in Q4. The council identifies this as a risk and attributes it to contractor performance delays in returning voids for letting. It is explicitly designated as 'one of the key priorities for the councils going forward' requiring a review of the full void process.
findings.matters: Void periods directly reduce HRA rental income; each property vacant at 84 rather than 60 days costs approximately 40 days of rent per turnover, with the council committed to improving this operational metric.
findings.figures: 84.13 days (actual Q1) vs 60 days (target)
findings.quote: Voids continue to be a risk to the councils and there have been challenges with contractors returning voids in a reasonable timeframe for properties to be let to new tenants. This is one of the key priorities for the councils going forward and we will be working with tenants to review the full void process.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Technical Assessments for Mid Suffolk Cabinet - September 2026
findings.headline: Elmswell to Woolpit project remains dependent on four critical approval conditions not yet fully secured, particularly National Highways agreement on A14 overbridge design.
findings.detail: The project cannot proceed without: National Highways final approval for the A14 overbridge section; dedication of land not currently owned by highways; bilateral funding mechanism between councils for s106 clawback; and regular stakeholder meetings. Geotechnical investigations and utility engagement are still ongoing and described as 'critical' to reducing construction risk.
findings.matters: Unmet preconditions for a £3.1m spend represent delivery risk. If National Highways approval is not granted or conditions cannot be secured before the March 2028 deadline, the CIL funding may be unspent and have to return to reserve, indicating failed capital deployment.
findings.figures: £3,099,930.16 at risk if five conditions not met; four conditions remain not fully agreed as of June 2026.
findings.quote: The CIL bid award is subject to National Highways providing final approval/agreement to the design of the section of the route that makes use of the A14 overbridge.

findings.paper_title: MSDC Cabinet Report September 2026 New version(V1)
findings.headline: The Ringfenced Infrastructure Fund has £24m available but only 30% of collected ringfenced funds have been allocated to projects since 2016, indicating slower capital deployment than planned.
findings.detail: The fund has collected £34.3m from major housing developments since April 2016 but only £11.4m (30%) has been allocated to infrastructure projects to support those developments, with £1.2m deallocated due to deadline expiry or underspend. This leaves £24m in available funds. Similar patterns appear in the Strategic Infrastructure Fund (67% allocated) and Local Infrastructure Fund (34% allocated).
findings.matters: Large accumulations of unspent developer-contributed infrastructure funding suggest the council may be unable to deploy capital at the pace expected by developers, which could affect future developer willingness to invest and the council's ability to support growth.
findings.figures: Ringfenced Fund collected £34,262,114.27, allocated £11,421,628.63 (30%), deallocated £1,177,808.33, currently available £24,024,052.86

findings.paper_title: MSDC Cabinet Report September 2026 New version(V1)
findings.headline: The Woolpit and Elmswell footway and cycleway project requires a nine-month deadline extension because its design phase overran the expected timeline.
findings.detail: The £3.1m CIL-funded project (part of a £3.5m total scheme) was originally approved in June 2025 with a standard 2-year completion deadline (expiring June 2027). Cabinet is now asked to extend this to 31 March 2028. The delay is attributed to the design phase taking longer than expected. The project is also dependent on National Highways approval, land dedication, and a funding clawback mechanism with Suffolk County Council.
findings.matters: A major capital project running behind schedule after only 12-15 months into a 2-year delivery window signals capital project delivery and inter-agency coordination challenges that could affect other council commitments.
findings.figures: £3,099,930.16 CIL; total project cost £3,498,425.00; additional funding from S106 (£398,494.84) and SCC Active Travel (£300,000)
findings.quote: Given that the design phase has taken longer than expected to conclude, it is clear that without an extension of time it would not be possible to draw down all the CIL funds to complete the project before the expiry of the 2-year period which expires on the 10th of June 2027

findings.paper_title: MSDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Reserves drawn down to fund capital; opening reserves £49.2m, forecast closing £33.9m
findings.detail: Opening reserves at 1 April 2026 were £49.2m (higher than the budgeted £40.4m because of 2025/26 capital underspends). The forecast closing position is £33.9m. Of the £37m at end Q1, £5.895m has already been used to fund the capital programme. Reserves are declining in nominal terms and being consumed to fund capital rather than building resilience.
findings.matters: While reserves remain substantial, the pattern of drawdown to fund capital (rather than cash generation from operations) shows the council is mining reserves rather than living within means. At current trajectory, this limits headroom for shocks.
findings.figures: Opening 1 April 2026: £49.2m. Q1 position: £37m (after £5.895m capital funding). Forecast closing 31 March 2027: £33.9m.
findings.quote: The reserves position at the end of quarter one is £ 37m, which includes the addition of the year to date surplus of £710k and the funding of the capital programme £5.895m.

findings.paper_title: MSDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Finance directorate forecasting £1.5m overspend; audit delivery requiring extra resource
findings.detail: The Finance & Procurement directorate's forecast shows £1.5m overspend (£538k YTD variance of £1.5m full year). Commentary cites 'additional resource to meet audit delivery' and notes the Housing Benefits overspend is due to temporary accommodation costs exceeding government limits. The requirement for additional resource to meet audit delivery suggests audit issues or regulatory findings.
findings.matters: A finance function needing extra resources to deliver audit is a signal of either audit findings or control weakness; the council is also reaching the ceiling on what government allows for Housing Benefit spend on temporary accommodation.
findings.figures: Finance & Procurement £1.5m full-year overspend (£538k YTD)
findings.quote: Financial Resources – Overspend on staff costs from additional resource to meet audit delivery and not achieving the vacancy management factor.

findings.paper_title: MSDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Borrowing rising sharply: outstanding debt forecast to reach £123.4m (up £30.6m in one year)
findings.detail: Actual debt at March 2026 was £92.8m. The forecast for March 2027 is £123.4m—a £30.6m increase in a single financial year. Financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream are rising from 10% to 15% in that same period, and budgeted to reach 20% by 2028/29. The council states it will not incur new borrowing for the General Fund capital programme in 2026/27, but HRA borrowing is tracking sharply upward (£129m to £145m).
findings.matters: Borrowing is rising faster than revenue; at current trajectory, financing costs will consume 20p of every pound of council tax, business rates and grants by 2028/29. This is a structural squeeze that limits service capacity and borrowing headroom.

The variance means less money available to rebuild reserves or fund capital.
findings.matters: Forecast outturn shows the council's financial planning assumptions are not holding; this reduces financial flexibility and limits the ability to respond to future shocks.

findings.matters: Company performance weaker than forecast suggests business plans are underperforming; the council is dependent on trading company returns to balance its accounts and those returns are not materialising.

findings.paper_title: MSDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Employee costs forecast to overspend by £291k; vacancy management targets not being hit
findings.detail: The council budgeted for salary savings through a vacancy management factor, but multiple service areas are failing to achieve it. Agency costs are covering an Interim Director of Housing; one-off restructuring costs are also materialising. A £68k underspend at Q1 is expected to reverse to a £291k full-year overspend.
findings.matters: A council unable to hold budgeted vacancies suggests either organisational instability or roles that cannot be left empty; agency cover and temporary appointments are more expensive and less stable than permanent staffing.
findings.figures: £291k full-year employee overspend; £68k Q1 underspend reversing to overspend
findings.quote: On the current trajectory the Council would not achieve the vacancy management factor. This is in part due to agency costs covering the Interim Director of Housing, the one off costs associated with restructures and several service areas not achieving the vacancy management factor.

findings.paper_title: MSDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Bed and breakfast costs for temporary accommodation climbing £412k above budget
findings.detail: The council is forecasting an additional £412k spend on B&B costs in the current year, driven by temporary accommodation pressures. This feeds into a £117k overspend in Housing Solutions year-end. The paper notes separately that £5m is forecast to be spent in 2026/27 on purchasing temporary accommodation for the General Fund, suggesting a strategic shift to owned stock rather than rented.
findings.matters: Homelessness pressures are acute and rising; the council is committing significant capital and revenue to accommodation, which is a constraint on other services and raises questions about demand drivers and sustainability.
findings.figures: £412k additional B&B spend, £117k Housing Solutions overspend, £5m temporary accommodation purchase forecast
findings.quote: Supplies and services are currently overspent by £189k year to date. The current full year forecast is an overspend of £986k, this is as a result of additional spend on bed & breakfast costs of £412k and costs in Strategic Planning relating to Local Plans of £294k.

findings.paper_title: BDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Capital programme £11.7m majority funded by borrowing, increasing MRP costs in 2027/28 and beyond
findings.detail: Full-year capital expenditure forecast £11.674m, with borrowing of £5.577m (49% of programme). Council notes 'The majority of the capital programme is funded by borrowing which will increase MRP in 2027/28.' Borrowing is already at £123.6m, and the Proportion of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream is forecast 30% in 2026/27 (up from 26% in 2025/26) and 32% in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Increasing capital borrowing while annual position has turned to deficit and reserves are falling creates a tightening cash position. MRP costs rising to 32% of net revenue stream leaves diminishing headroom for service delivery and reduces borrowing capacity for future contingencies.
findings.figures: Capital borrowing £5.577m in 2026/27; financing costs 30% of net revenue stream (forecast 32% in 2027/28)
findings.quote: The majority of the capital programme is funded by borrowing which will increase MRP in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: BDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Employee costs forecast £267k over budget as vacancy management factor not achieved
findings.detail: £88k adverse variance year-to-date, with full-year forecast £267k overspend on employee costs. Reasons cited: agency costs for Interim Director of Housing, one-off restructure costs, and 'several service areas not achieving the vacancy management factor'. The council explicitly states 'On the current trajectory the Council would not achieve the vacancy management factor', indicating inability to deliver planned efficiencies.
findings.matters: Vacancy management factors are a standard tool to create headroom in budgets; if the council cannot achieve them, it signals staffing inefficiencies or inability to implement planned headcount reductions. This is a structural cost control problem, not a one-off issue.
findings.figures: £267k full-year forecast overspend on employee costs
findings.quote: If this trend continues, the forecast position for the year would be a forecast overspend of £267k against budget. On the current trajectory the Council would not achieve the vacancy management factor.

findings.paper_title: BDC 26.27 Q1 GF Outturn Cabinet Final
findings.headline: Borehamgate Shopping Centre rental income collapsed to 61% of budget due to high void rates
findings.detail: Rental income for Borehamgate Shopping Centre forecast to be only 61% of budgeted amount due to under-occupancy. findings.matters: A council-owned commercial asset producing only 61% of expected income raises questions about asset valuation on the balance sheet, management capability, and asset quality. findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in homelessness services signal unmet service need and indicate this budget line will continue to exceed expectations. The council is absorbing costs it cannot refuse, reducing headroom elsewhere.
findings.figures: Housing Solutions £156k forecast overspend, Temporary Accommodation £54k, B&B shortfall £17k, Guaranteed Rent Scheme voids £38k
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation is forecasting to overspend by £54k due to less funding and higher demand. findings.matters: The council's own risk assessment acknowledges potential unsustainability; the proposed mitigation (cutting development programme) directly conflicts with the need to replace RTB losses and grow income.

findings.quote: HRA: Mid Suffolk District Council may fail to be financially sustainable

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Babergh CIL Expenditure Programme - September 2026

findings.paper_title: Joint TM Outturn Report Reviewed (1)
findings.headline: Babergh's short-term borrowing is £43.5m and requires refinancing at elevated rates, with 35% of debt maturing within 12 months
findings.detail: Babergh increased short-term borrowing from local authorities by £4.5m to £43.5m in 2025/26. Short-term rates were 4.0%-4.5% for most of the year but rose to 5.0%-7.0% towards end of financial year. With 35.19% of Babergh's total debt maturing within 12 months, the council faces significant refinancing exposure if rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing matures quickly and must be refinanced; if elevated rates persist, debt servicing costs will increase further, further squeezing already-pressured budgets.
findings.figures: £43.5m short-term borrowing (up £4.5m from £39m), rates 4.0%-7.0%, 35.19% of Babergh debt maturing within 12 months
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been similar to or a little above Base Rate for most of the period, with interest rates between 4.0% and 4.5%. However, as is commonly seen, rates rose higher towards the end of the financial year, with rates of 5.0% - 7.0%.

findings.paper_title: Joint TM Outturn Report Reviewed (1)
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk's Needham Market housing scheme phase 2 was cancelled after incurring £877k in costs
findings.detail: Phase 2 of Mid Suffolk's housing development at the former council offices in Needham Market has been cancelled. Costs of £877k were written off in the 2025/26 accounts. Phase 2 land has been sold for £2.7m, with the development agreement scheduled to formally close in 2026/27. Phase 1 was completed but generated only £321k land receipt and £281k dividend.
findings.matters: A second capital scheme failure within the council group (alongside Babergh's ongoing Hadleigh losses) indicates broader execution risk on commercial property investments and capital schemes.
findings.figures: £877k written off, £2.7m land sale proceeds, original scheme at Needham Market
findings.quote: Phase two of the development has been cancelled, having incurred costs of £877k which were written off in the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts. Phase 2 land has now been sold off by the Council for £2.7m.

findings.paper_title: Joint TM Outturn Report Reviewed (1)
findings.headline: CIFCO Ltd is deferring interest payments to the councils and carries £434k expected credit loss per council
findings.detail: Both councils have advanced £43m in loans to CIFCO Ltd, their commercial property investment vehicle. CIFCO is paying interest in arrears and the business plan permits 10% deferment of interest to support cash flow while asset sales proceed. Treasury advisors have calculated the expected credit loss (ECL) on these loans at £434k per council, though no MRP has been recognised pending expected future payments. Total interest deferred across both councils is £1.3m to date.
findings.matters: Deferred income from a council's own commercial lending entity signals cash flow stress; the ECL provision indicates credit deterioration risk that could force additional provisions or limit dividend availability.
findings.figures: £1.3m total interest deferred to date, 10% deferment permitted in business plan, £434k ECL per council, £43m loans per council
findings.quote: CIFCO are paying interest due in arrears and in the current business plan a 10% deferment of interest repayments has been noted will be permitted to aid cashflow whilst sales and any necessary works are being delivered by CIFCO

findings.paper_title: Joint TM Outturn Report Reviewed (1)
findings.headline: Babergh's housing development at Hadleigh is now expected to result in £4.889m unrecoverable loan loss
findings.detail: Babergh Growth Ltd received loans of £12.8m (facility approved to increase to £13.7m) for housing development. The council now expects £4.889m of the loan will not be repaid. The expected credit loss has been increased from £3.1m (prior year) to £4.889m, resulting in a £1.213m MRP charge funded by drawing £938k from the ECL Reserve and £275k from the Pooled Fund Reserve. Although practical completion has been achieved, not all housing units have been sold, and the final loss will not be known until later in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that Babergh is exposed to significant capital scheme losses and is drawing reserves to cover them, indicating tightening cash position and reduced financial resilience.
findings.figures: £4.889m expected unrecoverable, £1.213m MRP charge for year, £12.8m current facility with £13.7m approved, £938k + £275k drawn from reserves
findings.quote: Based on current projections, the Council does not expect around £4.889m of the loan to be repaid. An ECL of £3.1m was recognised in the 2024/25 accounts. This now needs to be increased to £4.889m.

findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation demand surge depletes dedicated reserve to zero

findings.detail: Waste contract overspent by £387k in 2025/26 due to increases in contracted officer pay agreed in Q2 plus above-inflation contract uplift. This sits within the £222k net overspend on major contracts. A new waste service is launching June 2026, which will shift cost base further.
findings.matters: Waste is a core statutory service and the overspend signals embedded cost pressures that will recur. The pay settlement and contract terms may lock the council into higher bases for future years.

findings.quote: An increase in major contract costs by £222k of which £387k is from the Waste contract due to increase contracted officer pay agreed during quarter two and an above inflation increase in the contract.

findings.paper_title: BDC HRA Outturn Final
findings.headline: Strategic Reserves drawn down by £2.470m to fund revenue deficit, reducing reserve cover from £14.856m to £12.386m

findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to cover annual deficits limits financial flexibility and indicates the HRA is structurally dependent on reserves rather than operating profitably; over time this constrains the council's ability to invest and respond to shocks.
