findings.paper_title: MSDC HRA Outturn Final
findings.headline: Damp and mould remediation costs exploded from budget
findings.detail: Budgeted at £24k, actual spending reached £445k — a 18-fold overspend. The council notes these are increased costs for repairs, surveys and cleaning. Whilst stated as covered by repairs underspends, it signals serious property condition issues requiring sustained spending.
findings.matters: Asset condition deterioration drives long-term maintenance costs and suggests the housing stock may have systemic problems; unexpected cost escalations reduce reserve flexibility.
findings.figures: £24k budget vs £445k actual (£421k overspend)
findings.quote: Increase in Damp and Mould costs for repairs, surveys and cleaning. Overspend to be covered by underspend on repairs.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: 14 high-risk audit findings raised; 85 findings total with governance and process weaknesses as leading causes
findings.detail: The audit identified 85 findings across the council: 14 high-risk, 48 medium, 23 low. Root cause analysis shows 31% stem from Processes & Procedures failures, 16% from Governance gaps, and 16% from Assurance & Monitoring weaknesses, indicating systemic control design and operational issues rather than isolated incidents.
findings.matters: Multiple high-risk findings indicate material control weaknesses requiring urgent management action; the concentration in processes, governance and assurance suggests the council's control framework has significant design or operational gaps.
findings.figures: 14 High, 48 Medium, 23 Low findings; 31% Processes & Procedures; 16% Governance; 16% Assurance & Monitoring root causes
findings.quote: In 2025/26, 85 findings were raised: High ( 14): Findings that highlight significant control weaknesses or increased risk. Management should be implementing agreed actions as soon as possible.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing data integrity failure: misnamed and missing gas safety reports created severe risk of uninspected properties
findings.detail: The Gas Policy audit identified a data integrity failure where a misnamed and missing valid Landlord Gas Safety Report created the severe risk of an uninspected and potentially dangerous property. Testing also found the issuance of tenant gas safety certificates within the 28-day legal period could not be verified, representing a compliance blind spot and potential regulatory risk.
findings.matters: Gas safety compliance is a statutory health and safety requirement; missing records mean uninspected properties could pose severe tenant safety risks and regulatory liability; inability to verify 28-day certificates means no assurance of legal compliance despite reported 99.6% completion rates.
findings.figures: 99.64% completion rate reported for Babergh; but data quality failure found; compliance verification impossible for 28-day certificate issuance
findings.quote: A data integrity failure was identified where a misnamed and missing valid Landlord Gas Safety Report (LGSR) created the severe risk of an uninspected and potentially dangerous property... The issuance of Tenant gas safety certificates within the 28 - day period could not be verified, representing a compliance blind spot and potential regulatory risk.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Procurement contracts register incomplete with 6 already-expired contracts; procurement records incomplete for audit verification
findings.detail: The Procurement Process audit found the published contracts register does not contain all required information under the Local Government Transparency Code 2015, and includes 6 contracts that have already expired. For the sample reviewed, multiple required procurement documents could not be obtained, preventing audit assurance over compliance with Public Contracts Regulations 2015.
findings.matters: Contract transparency and proper records are statutory requirements; missing contracts and incomplete records prevent oversight of spend, expose the council to legal challenge on procurement decisions, and prevent audit verification of regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: 6 expired contracts in register; multiple documents unable to be located for sample testing; Transparency Code compliance failing
findings.quote: The published contracts registers do not contain all required information as per Local Government Transparency Code 2015, and do not include all required information there are six contracts which have already expired... For the chosen sample to be reviewed, multiple documents could not be obtained, resulting in Internal Audit not being able to give assurance over some areas of the PCR.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Payments process allows budget approvers to approve their own payment vouchers, creating segregation of duties failure
findings.detail: The Payments Process audit raised an urgent recommendation that requisitioners who are also the budget code approver are able to approve their own payment vouches, and that supplier amendments completed within procurement do not undergo verification by a second member of staff. These were identified as high-risk control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties is a fundamental financial control; allowing individuals to approve their own spending creates fraud risk and was raised as an urgent (high-risk) finding requiring immediate system controls.
findings.figures: One urgent high-risk recommendation per finding; follow-up completed with recommendations now fully implemented
findings.quote: An urgent recommendation has been raised in relation to requisitioners who are also the approver of the budget code being able to approve their own payment vouchers requisitions. Appropriate system controls need to be put into place to address this.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Section 151 statutory financial reports not produced since April 2024 Unit4 migration
findings.detail: The Payments Process audit found that Section 151 reports, required under statute, have not been completed since the April 2024 move to Unit4. The submission deadline for 2024/2025 was 30 May 2025. This represents a gap of over a year in a key statutory reporting requirement for local authority finance oversight.
findings.matters: Section 151 reports are a statutory requirement and fundamental to demonstrating proper financial governance; their non-production since April 2024 means the council lacks a key control on its own financial position and external audit relies on this reporting.
findings.figures: Deadline: 30 May 2025; reports missing since April 2024
findings.quote: The Section 151 reports have not been completed since the move to the system Unit 4 in April 2024. The submission deadline for 2024/2025, was 30 May 2025.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 V6
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk facing cliff-edge financial pressure in 2029/30 despite medium-term surpluses
findings.detail: Mid Suffolk is currently forecasting surpluses over the next three years (2026/27 onwards), but faces a significant budget cliff when the three-year spending review ends. A budget gap of £954k is forecast for 2029/30, increasing to £2.2m in 2030/31. The council also faces £2.271m Government funding reduction over the three-year period.
findings.matters: The combination of core spending power reduction (-3% over three years) and a significant cliff-edge budget gap in 2029/30 represents medium-term financial sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £954k budget gap 2029/30; £2.2m gap 2030/31; £2.271m Government funding reduction over three years; core spending power reduces by 3% over three years
findings.quote: Despite this the Council is forecasting surpluses over the next three years but a cliff edge at the end of the three-year spending review in 2029/30 with a budget gap of £954k increasing to £2.2m in 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 V6
findings.headline: Procurement team vacancies and resource constraints delayed service development and capacity
findings.detail: Two Procurement Business Partner posts had vacancies during 2024/25, with one position vacant until December. External auditor has reported this as a significant weakness. Challenges recruiting skilled interim and permanent staff in the market impacted the team's capacity to provide service and progress service development.
findings.matters: Unfilled procurement roles in a team already facing audit criticism creates ongoing risk of non-compliance and poor contract management during a period of high spend.
findings.figures: Two Procurement Business Partner posts with vacancy period until December 2024; total procurement spend and contracts noted above
findings.quote: The challenges to recruit skilled interim and permanent posts in the current market have impacted on the capacity to provide a service and service development progress.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 V6
findings.headline: Multiple internal audits of procurement and finance controls issued Limited Assurance ratings
findings.detail: Three separate internal audits in 2025/26 resulted in Limited Assurance opinions: Contract Management and Spend (August 2025), Procurement Payments Process (September 2025), and Procurement Process (January 2026). The Procurement Process audit found that multiple documents could not be obtained for review, making it impossible to confirm correct procurement routes were followed.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance findings across procurement controls and contract management over a short period indicate systemic weaknesses in procurement governance and records management affecting value for money.
findings.figures: Three Limited Assurance audits within six months; total spend 2024/25 was £59.8m with 1,201 suppliers; 181 contracts on register valued at £39m
findings.quote: For the chosen sample to be reviewed, multiple documents could not be obtained, resulting in Internal Audit not being able to give assurance over some areas of the PCR. It was not possible to establish if correct procurement route had been complied with.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 V6
findings.headline: Finance function inherited interim-heavy staffing and required additional resource business case
findings.detail: The Head of Finance inherited a team with several roles covered by interims. The S151 Officer and Head of Finance submitted a business case for approval to address finance function resourcing for the 2025/26 year-end process. The team has now recruited more permanent qualified officers.
findings.matters: Reliance on interim staff in finance, coupled with acknowledgment that additional permanent resources are needed, indicates staffing weakness that contributed to audit support failures and may persist.
findings.figures: Unspecified number of interim roles in inherited finance team; additional resources required for 2025/26 and beyond
findings.quote: The Head of Finance has now recruited more permanent qualified officers into the team, having inherited a team with several roles covered by interims.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 V6
findings.headline: Babergh faces £9.9m unfunded medium-term gap against £6.5m available reserves
findings.detail: Babergh has identified a cumulative budget gap of £9.9m over the medium term, with only £6.5m in the financial resilience and risk reserve available. This follows £1.367m of savings in 2026/27 and a £633k budget gap in 2025/26. The council's core spending power only increases by 0.3% over three years while pay and contractual inflation will not be covered.
findings.matters: An identified structural gap substantially larger than available reserves represents a material financial sustainability risk requiring significant further savings or service reductions.
findings.figures: £9.9m medium-term gap; £6.5m in reserves; £1.4m Government funding reduction over three years; 0.3% core spending power increase over three-year period
findings.quote: The gap over the medium-term totals £9.9m and with only £6.5m in the financial resilience and risk reserve, further work will be carried out in 2026/27 to address this.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 V6
findings.headline: External auditor issuing statutory recommendation on accounts process and unable to complete detailed audit procedures
findings.detail: Ernst & Young have disclaimed audit opinions on accounts for 2020/21 through to 2023/24 due to time constraints. For 2024/25, the auditor states they cannot complete detailed audit procedures needed to issue an unmodified report. The auditor is making a statutory recommendation under Section 7 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 in relation to the accounts process.
findings.matters: Inability to obtain clean audit opinions over four years, and ongoing issues with 2024/25 accounts, indicates fundamental weakness in finance function capability to support external audit and prepare compliant financial statements.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2020/21-2023/24); 2024/25 accounts could not be fully audited due to timing/evidence constraints
findings.quote: EY reported in their independent audit report that due to the disclaimers of opinion on the financial statements in the prior years, delays in receiving associated audit evidence and the Councils inability to support the audit in advance of the backstop date, they have not been able to complete the detailed audit procedures that would be needed to obtain an unmodified audit report

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Going concern risks for Council subsidiaries requiring significant judgement
findings.detail: Several Council subsidiaries have going concern positions that require significant judgement due to operating losses and reliance on forecasted funding. The auditor has identified this as a new inherent risk for 2025/26, with risk that going concern disclosures may be inadequate.
findings.matters: Subsidiaries with uncertain going concern status that are consolidated into the Group accounts could require write-down or restructuring. Inadequate disclosure of these risks misstates the Group's true financial position.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: The Council has a number of subsidiaries whose going concern positions require judgement, particularly in light of operating losses and reliance on funding and forecasts.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: HRA depreciation policy change (useful life extended from 35 to 50 years) not yet audited, carried forward from 2024/25
findings.detail: The Council is changing its HRA (Housing Revenue Account) depreciation policy, extending the useful economic life of assets from 35 to 50 years, which reduces annual depreciation charges. This represents a change in accounting policy. The auditor could not conclude on this in 2024/25 and has carried it forward as an inherent risk.
findings.matters: A 43% extension to asset lives directly reduces reported depreciation costs and increases reported asset values. Without audit conclusion, it is unknown whether the change is justifiable and properly accounted for.
findings.figures: HRA Depreciation 2024/25: £3.7m
findings.quote: We have noted in prior year that the Council plans to change its depreciation policy for HRA assets. The change increases the estimated useful life of the assets from 35 to 50 years. As this is a change in accounting policy, we have raised an inherent risk for this.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) accounting: material errors found in 2019/20 (unspent CIL misclassified as reserves instead of creditors/unapplied grants)
findings.detail: In 2019/20, the auditor found that the Council was incorrectly recognising unspent CIL income in Earmarked Reserves instead of Capital Grants Unapplied Account and Creditors. This risk remains active because no audit procedures have been completed since 2019/20. Current CIL reserves/creditors balance is £49.3m.
findings.matters: CIL income is restricted to specific infrastructure purposes. Misclassification overstates available reserves and understates restricted liabilities, materially misstating the Council's true financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Grants Unapplied Reserves: £49.3m in 2024/25 (prior year £44.4m)
findings.quote: Our work in 2019/20 audit identified a number of adjustments to the Council's accounts, including material amendments, where the Council incorrectly recognised the unspent CIL income in Earmarked Reserves instead of Capital Grants Unapplied Account and Creditors.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: IFRS 16 leases implementation not concluded in 2024/25, carried forward as significant risk
findings.detail: IFRS 16 requires recognition of lease assets and liabilities on the balance sheet (rather than off-balance-sheet as operating leases). The auditor was unable to assess the Council's transition in 2024/25 and is carrying this forward as a significant risk for 2025/26. Successful implementation requires complete capture of lease information and new systems for cost tracking.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 could result in material new assets and liabilities appearing on the Council's balance sheet. Failure to correctly implement this standard could materially misstate the reported financial position.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: As we weren't able to assess the Council's transition to the new standard, hence, this procedure will be carried forward in 25/26.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Prior material valuation errors in land and buildings (identified in 2019/20) remain unresolved due to five years of disclaimed opinions
findings.detail: The auditor notes that 2019/20 audit identified material valuation errors in land and buildings (which represent £351m of total property, plant and equipment). Because no audit procedures have been completed since 2019/20, these errors have not been followed up or resolved. The Council is now implementing CIPFA Bulletin 22 (new valuation guidance) but with historical valuation gaps unresolved.
findings.matters: Unresolved material errors in asset valuations from six years ago that have not been subject to audit procedures since then create fundamental uncertainty about the Council's asset base and net worth.
findings.figures: Land and buildings: £351m total; additions in 24/25: £16m; related PPE balance £336m
findings.quote: The 2019/20 audit identified material valuation errors in these assets... During 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25, we were not able to complete any planned audit procedures

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Finance system migration from Integra to Unit4 at 1 April 2024 carries material misstatement risk not yet concluded
findings.detail: The Council migrated its finance system on 1 April 2024. The auditor could not conclude on this risk in 2024/25 and has carried it forward as a significant risk for 2025/26. Risk includes data loss, incomplete recording of entries, and incorrect system configuration affecting all financial statement balances.
findings.matters: A failed or poorly executed system migration can cause systematic errors across an entire year's accounts. The Council has now operated Unit4 for 12 months but the auditor has not yet achieved assurance over the completeness and accuracy of data.
findings.figures: Impacts all financial statement balances
findings.quote: The Council had a change in finance system at the start of the year (1 April 2024). They have changed their system from Integra to Unit4... As we weren't able to conclude on this area in 24/25, this risk had been carried forward for 25/26.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Material subsidiary risks: CIFCO Capital Ltd revenue of £6.4m (fraud risk) and investment property of £81.4m (valuation risk)
findings.detail: The Council accounts for CIFCO using equity accounting. CIFCO recognised £6.4m of material revenue (fraud risk, presumed under audit standards) and holds £81.4m of investment property requiring fair value assessment. Any misstatement at CIFCO flows directly into the Council's consolidated results.
findings.matters: These are material balances (£6.4m revenue, £81.4m property) passing through the Council's group accounts. Misstatement of CIFCO's revenue recognition or property valuations directly misstates the Council's reported financial position by equity accounting.
findings.figures: CIFCO Capital Ltd: £6.4m revenue, £81.4m investment property carrying value
findings.quote: CIFCO Capital Ltd recognised £6.4m of revenue for the year ended 31 March 2025, which is material to its results and impacts the Council through equity accounting... CIFCO Capital Ltd holds investment property with a carrying value of £81.4m, which is material to its financial statements and impacts the Council through equity accounting.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Recharges between Babergh and Mid Suffolk identified as fraud risk due to financial pressure and joint arrangement
findings.detail: The auditor has identified recharges between the two councils as a specific fraud risk, noting that these could be manipulated to increase or reduce each council's reported financial position, given the joint working arrangement and the respective financial pressures of each council.
findings.matters: If recharges can be manipulated by management to change reported financial position, the consolidated accounts are unreliable and lenders cannot trust the reported financial position of either authority.
findings.figures: Amounts not quantified in the document
findings.quote: there is a risk of management override in relation to the recharges between Babergh and Mid Suffolk. These recharges could be manipulated to increase or reduce the Council's reported financial position.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Contract management arrangements remain significantly weak despite years of recommendations
findings.detail: The auditor has identified a persistent significant weakness in contract management arrangements that has been reported in prior years without satisfactory resolution. Internal Audit has made recommendations on this for several years. This is classified as a risk of significant weakness in value for money arrangements.
findings.matters: Weak contract management exposes the Council to overpayment, non-compliance with procurement law, and inefficient use of public money — all material concerns for an authority managing significant spend.
findings.figures: No specific figures on value at risk
findings.quote: The risk of a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements around contract management is still applicable in the 2025/26 period... We note that Internal Audit have made recommendations in relation to contract management for several years.

findings.paper_title: 26 MSDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Council has not received an audited audit opinion on any of its accounts for five years (2020/21 through 2024/25)
findings.detail: The auditor has disclaimed opinions on every set of accounts since 2020/21, unable to complete any planned audit procedures due to delays in receiving evidence and the Council's inability to support the audit in advance of backstop dates. The most recent unqualified opinion was issued for 2019/20. This is the foundational issue shaping the entire 2025/26 audit strategy.
findings.matters: For a lender deciding whether to lend, lack of verified accounts for five years means no audited view of the Council's true financial position, and is a material counterparty risk.
findings.quote: During 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25, we were not able to complete any planned audit procedures and therefore have not been able to start any "natural" rebuild.

findings.paper_title: 26 BDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Contract management weaknesses persisted for multiple years without resolution
findings.detail: The auditor notes that a significant weakness in contract management arrangements identified in prior years remains present. Internal Audit has made recommendations in relation to contract management for several years without apparent resolution. The auditor recommends the Joint Audit and Standards Committee monitor progress on implementing clear strategies, policies and procedures for procurement compliance.
findings.matters: Unresolved multi-year control weaknesses suggest either limited management capacity or insufficient priority given to addressing them; weak contract management exposes the council to procurement breaches, value-for-money failures, and potential clawback of grant funding.
findings.figures: Weakness identified in prior years; multiple years of Internal Audit recommendations without implementation
findings.quote: The significant weakness identified in the prior years regarding the Council's contract management arrangement is still present.

findings.paper_title: 26 BDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Internal Audit findings show weaknesses in segregation of duties and payment controls
findings.detail: A risk of significant weakness has been identified in the council's governance arrangements arising from limited assurance Internal Audit findings over the payment process. The findings highlight weaknesses in segregation of duties, verification controls and statutory reporting, which reduce assurance over the effectiveness of governance and oversight.
findings.matters: Weak payment controls and poor segregation of duties create fraud risk and indicate that the control environment may not be preventing or detecting errors and irregularities; this has direct bearing on the reliability of reported expenditure.
findings.figures: Limited assurance rating from Internal Audit on payment process
findings.quote: A risk of significant weakness has been identified in relation to the Council's governance arrangements, arising from limited assurance Internal Audit findings over the payment process. These findings highlight weaknesses in segregation of duties, verification controls and statutory reporting, reducing assurance over the effectiveness of governance and oversight.

findings.paper_title: 26 BDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Finance system migration from Integra to Unit4 remains unaudited and is a significant risk
findings.detail: The council migrated its finance system from Integra to Unit4 at 1 April 2024. The auditor notes this was a significant risk in 2024/25 (which was not audited) and has been carried forward as a significant risk for 2025/26. The risk is that information may be incorrectly transferred or reported in the financial statements.
findings.matters: A major finance system change that has not been audited means there is unverified risk of material reporting errors; if the data migration was flawed, underlying transactions and balances could be incorrect.
findings.figures: System change on 1 April 2024
findings.quote: As we were not able to conclude on this area in 2024/25, this risk had been carried forward for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 26 BDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: No audit procedures completed for five consecutive years; opening balances now unknowable
findings.detail: The auditor explicitly states that during 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 they were unable to complete any planned audit procedures on Babergh's financial statements. This means there is a material risk that the opening reserves balances at 1 April 2025 are materially misstated. The auditor will undertake a detailed risk assessment of the opening position but has indicated it is unlikely they will commence rebuilding assurance over the historic five-year position during 2025/26.
findings.matters: A council's opening balances are the starting point for all future financial reporting; five years of unaudited balances mean the council's reported financial position is unverified and potentially unreliable for decision-making.
findings.figures: Five years of disclaimed audit opinions (2020/21 through 2024/25)
findings.quote: During 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25, we were not able to complete any planned audit procedures and therefore have not been able to start any 'natural' rebuild.

findings.paper_title: 26 BDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Babergh Growth Ltd is in net liability position with £3 million loan repayment shortfall forecast
findings.detail: The council holds an investment in Babergh Growth Ltd which has incurred ongoing losses and is in net liability. The auditor identified this as a new significant risk. Separately, the council has provided a loan to Babergh Growth with a forecasted shortfall in repayments of £3 million—a material figure. The auditor will assess whether the investment is impaired and whether expected credit loss on the loan is understated.
findings.matters: A trading subsidiary in loss-making position with material unrecoverable lending represents a value destruction event; the council may need to inject capital or absorb losses that further compress its financial position.
findings.figures: £3 million forecasted repayment shortfall on Babergh Growth loan; Babergh Growth in net liability position
findings.quote: In the MTFS reported to the Cabinet on 10 February 2026, the forecasted shortfall in repayments is £3 million, which is material, and there is a risk regarding repayment of this loan.

findings.paper_title: 26 BDC LG 225UK Provisional Audit Planning Report
findings.headline: Reserves projected to run out by 2029/30 as funding gap continues to widen
findings.detail: The auditor identifies a significant weakness risk in financial sustainability. The council faces a growing gap between budget requirements and available funding, and plans to use earmarked reserves to cover the shortfall. These reserves are expected to be completely depleted within three years. The council will need to identify material savings or income increases to avoid this.
findings.matters: A council burning through reserves on a finite timeline is a direct credit risk; lenders need to know whether the gap will be closed by service transformation or simply postponed until reserves run out.
findings.figures: Reserves fully depleted by 2029/30
findings.quote: The Council anticipates that the gap between its budget requirement and available funding will continue to grow. To address this shortfall, the Council plans to use its earmarked reserves. However, these reserves are expected to be fully depleted by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/37 2026-27 GF MSDC COUNCIL Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Pension fund contribution rate reduction to 16.4% delivers £1.116m saving but next review not until 2029/30
findings.detail: Actuaries' revaluation of the pension fund allowed the contribution rate to be reduced from 26% to 16.4% for 2026/27, delivering a £1.116m saving. This is a material positive adjustment to the budget. However, the next review is scheduled for 2029/30, so this benefit is locked in for only three years with potential for future increases.
findings.matters: Pension fund valuations directly impact the council's revenue budget; a negative revaluation in 2029/30 could reverse this £1.116m benefit and create financial pressure.
findings.figures: Contribution rate reduced from 26% to 16.4%; £1.116m saving; next revaluation 2029/30
findings.quote: the latest Actuaries revaluation of the pension fund confirmed that the rate could be reduced to 16.4% for 2026/27. This reduction equates to £1.116m.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/37 2026-27 GF MSDC COUNCIL Final Budget Report
findings.headline: New statutory food waste contract £1.602m annual cost from June 2026 is material new revenue commitment
findings.detail: From June 2026, the council will implement a national four-stream household collection system (residual waste, food waste, paper/card, dry recyclables) as a statutory requirement. This includes a new food waste contract of £1.602m and £1.2m in extended producer responsibility costs. The council is funding these from the Revenue Support Grant and reserves.
findings.matters: This represents a material new revenue commitment (£1.602m) driven by national policy rather than local choice, reducing the council's flexibility in financial management.
findings.figures: £1.602m food waste contract; £1.2m EPR funding
findings.quote: The major contracts budget for 2026/27 in table 5 includes the new Food Waste contract (£1.6m) and anticipated increases in the Domestic and Garden Waste contracts.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/37 2026-27 GF MSDC COUNCIL Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Council scheduled for abolition in 2028 as part of local government reorganisation creates planning uncertainty
findings.detail: The council has extended its current plan until its planned abolition in 2028 as part of the government's local government reorganisation policy creating new unitary councils across Suffolk. This creates a planning horizon of only two years for new initiatives, and raises questions about delivery of multi-year capital and strategic programmes after that point.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that financial and strategic commitments made now must be delivered or handed over within a constrained timeframe, and medium-term financial resilience depends on decisions made by bodies not yet in existence.
findings.figures: Council abolition scheduled 2028
findings.quote: Due to the planned establishment of new unitary councils throughout Suffolk in 2028 through the Government's Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) policy, it is proposed that the current Council Plan be extended until the abolition of the Council.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/37 2026-27 GF MSDC COUNCIL Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Council faces structural shift to deficit from 2029/30 as government core funding drops 35 percent
findings.detail: The medium-term financial plan forecasts the council switching from surplus to significant deficit from 2029/30 onwards. This is driven by planned loss of adjustment support grant (£1.061m from 2027/28) and transitional funding (£2.575m from 2029/30), together equating to a 35% reduction in core funding. The council is setting aside reserves (£194k in 2026/27) to mitigate this cliff edge.
findings.matters: The planned shift to deficit indicates underlying unsustainability of service delivery within forecast funding envelopes, a material financial risk regardless of the council's planned 2028 abolition.
findings.figures: 35% reduction in core funding; £1.061m adjustment support grant loss 2027/28; £2.575m transitional funding loss 2029/30; £194k set aside 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council will need to plan for the loss of the adjustment support grant in 2027/28 of £1.061m and the loss of transitional funding in 2029/30 of £2.575m, this equates to a 35% reduction in core funding from the 2026/27 level of funding.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/38 HRA MSDC COUNCIL Final budget report
findings.headline: Multiple regulatory requirements (Decent Homes 2, Awaab's Law, EPCC) drive capital and compliance cost pressures the HRA must absorb
findings.detail: The council faces overlapping regulatory pressures: the new Decent Homes Standard 2 (thermal comfort requirements), Awaab's Law (damp and mould liability), Energy Performance Certificate rating targets (EPCC compliance by 2030), and the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023. The report identifies these as part of 'significant challenges' and notes 'further legislation is expected this year', with capital programmes updated to reflect stock condition survey findings.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance drives capital expenditure (£19.367m budget for 2026/27) and ongoing operational costs that must be met regardless of HRA affordability or financial position; failure to comply creates reputational and enforcement risks for the council and its lenders.
findings.figures: 15% of stock currently non-decent homes; capital programme £19.367m in 2026/27; EPCC compliance required by 2030; Energy Performance Certificate E or below properties targeted for retrofit
findings.quote: Further legislation is expected this year, this includes Decent Homes two, which relates to the thermal comfort been updated and included in the plan.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/38 HRA MSDC COUNCIL Final budget report
findings.headline: Service charges on sheltered housing cannot achieve full cost recovery while maintaining tenant affordability
findings.detail: The council cannot recover full costs for sheltered housing services despite identifying additional recoverable charges, because 46% of sheltered tenants do not receive housing benefits and affordability is a constraint. The council is spreading cost increases over 4 years (£2.88/week service charge increase) to manage this, meaning the HRA is cross-subsidising sheltered services from general rental income.
findings.matters: Inability to achieve cost recovery on services indicates the HRA lacks pricing power and flexibility; it suggests either persistent operational inefficiency or that service delivery costs exceed the council's ability to charge vulnerable populations.
findings.figures: 46% of sheltered tenants not in receipt of housing benefits; service charge increase capped at 8% over 4 years (£2.88/week)
findings.quote: We recognise the importance of considering affordability for tenants. With 46% of tenants in sheltered housing not in receipt of housing benefits, we must balance fairness (ensuring services are not funded by general rental income) with affordability.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/38 HRA MSDC COUNCIL Final budget report
findings.headline: 44% of tenants receive Universal Credit paid direct to them, removing the council's visibility of rent support dependency
findings.detail: Of 3,463 tenants, 44.12% receive Universal Credit paid directly to the tenant rather than to the council. The council explicitly states it 'no longer knows the total number of tenants in receipt of support to pay their rent' because of this payment arrangement. Combined with 20.85% receiving Housing Benefit, this means roughly two-thirds of tenants depend on government housing support, but visibility of actual coverage is now incomplete.
findings.matters: Loss of visibility into tenant affordability and housing support creates rent collection risk, particularly with planned rent increases of 4.8% for social housing. Lenders rely on understanding tenant payment capacity.
findings.figures: 1,528 tenants (44.12%) on Universal Credit; 722 tenants (20.85%) on Housing Benefit; combined ~65% of 3,463 tenants dependent on support
findings.quote: As Universal Credit is paid direct to the tenant, rather than the landlord, the Council no longer knows the total number of tenants in receipt of support to pay their rent.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/38 HRA MSDC COUNCIL Final budget report
findings.headline: The HRA continues to run annual deficits funded by drawing down reserves by £906k in 2026/27
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget shows a deficit of £906k that will be funded from Strategic Priorities Reserves, following a 2025/26 forecast deficit of £1.622m. Whilst improving, this pattern shows the HRA is structurally spending more than it receives. Reserves are forecast to reach £2.654m by 31 March 2027 (£774 per property), with only £1m held as working balance.
findings.matters: Persistent annual deficits that drain reserves signal the HRA is not self-sustaining and raises questions about the longevity of reserve buffers, a key metric for lender confidence in the council's ability to weather financial shocks.
findings.figures: 2026/27 deficit £906k; 2025/26 forecast deficit £1.622m; total reserves 31 March 2027 £2.654m (£774 per property); working balance £1m (£300 per property)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget position means that the Council will reduce its Strategic Priorities Reserve by £906k, compared to the 2025/26 forecast reduction in reserves of £2.1m.

findings.paper_title: MC/25/38 HRA MSDC COUNCIL Final budget report
findings.headline: The 30-year business plan is not sustainable for its full term due to government rent convergence policy
findings.detail: The council's 30-year financial model, which is legally required to demonstrate HRA viability, will not remain sustainable across all 30 years. The government's decision to implement rent convergence at £1 per week for 2027/28 then £2 thereafter creates an adverse impact of £130k in 2027/28 alone, with the plan forecast to drop below the minimum working capital balance of £1m in years 29 and 30.
findings.matters: A business plan that fails to remain above minimum reserves for a material portion of its term indicates structural financial fragility; lenders rely on multi-year plans to assess council creditworthiness and this plan signals the HRA will face a solvency crisis within 30 years unless action is taken.
findings.figures: Plan unsustainable for full 30 years; drops below £1m minimum reserve in years 29-30; £130k adverse rent convergence impact in 2027/28
findings.quote: The long-term position in relation to the 30-year business plan, currently indicates that our position will not now be sustainable for the full 30 years following the Government's decision to implement a step change in rent convergence.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Significant restructuring of leisure services (Abbeycroft) increases council exposure and budget volatility
findings.detail: Abbeycroft Leisure has moved from a contracted service to an agency model, meaning the council now records both income and expenditure for leisure operations (Kingfisher and Hadleigh leisure centres) in its own budget. The leisure contract budget increased from £244k to £2,868k (a £2.6m increase). This restructuring concentrates leisure income and cost risk directly on the council and makes the budget more exposed to leisure usage volatility.
findings.matters: The council now directly owns the leisure income/cost risk; if leisure centres underperform, this flows directly to the council's revenue budget with no contractual buffer; a lender needs to understand the council is taking on more direct service delivery risk
findings.figures: Leisure contract budget increased from £244k (2025/26) to £2,868k (2026/27); includes Kingfisher (£1,762k) and Hadleigh (£912k)
findings.quote: The large increase in Leisure Contracts represents the change in model used with Abbeycroft Leisure moving to an agency model with income and expenditure now recorded in the Councils budgets.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Pay award assumptions carry material budget risk: each 1% above the 3% assumed creates £118k permanent pressure
findings.detail: The budget assumes 3% pay awards. A stress test shows that every additional 1% above this creates a permanent £118k budget pressure going forward. Given continued pay settlement uncertainties and the possibility that future awards could exceed assumptions, this is a key risk to the council's ability to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: Pay costs are the largest single budget item (£11.553m employee costs). A 1% variance above assumption, sustained across the workforce, is unaffordable within a council that is already facing a £9.656m five-year gap
findings.figures: 3% pay award assumed; £118k permanent budget pressure per additional 1% award; employees budget is £11.553m
findings.quote: A stress test on the budget has been completed illustrating that every 1% increase in the Pay Award creates a permanent and additional budget pressure of approximately £118k.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Major new food waste collection contract (£1.5m) dependent on Revenue Support Grant funding that is forecast to reduce over the MTFP period
findings.detail: From June 2026 the council will roll out a four-stream household collection system including food waste. The new food waste contract costs £1.5m and is funded by the Revenue Support Grant (RSG). However, RSG is forecast to reduce from £3.549m in 2026/27 to £3.071m in 2027/28 and £2.570m in 2028/29. If RSG reductions outpace EPR income, the council will have committed to an unaffordable service.
findings.matters: The council has created a multi-year cost (£1.5m waste contract) that depends on grant funding expected to reduce; if grant doesn't materialize or falls faster, the council cannot easily suspend waste collection
findings.figures: £1.5m food waste contract; £1m Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) new burdens funding; RSG reduces by £479k over 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: The budget includes new burdens funding for Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) of £1m. Funding for Food Waste will be supported by the Revenue Support Grant (RSG).

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Cliff in funding: £440k Adjustment Support Grant terminates in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council is receiving a one-off Adjustment Support Grant of £440k in 2026/27 to help it through a business rates reset. This terminates in 2027/28, creating an immediate £440k hole in the following year's budget that must be covered through new savings or income.
findings.matters: The 2026/27 surplus of £334k is partly dependent on the Adjustment Support Grant; without it, the position reverts to deficit, and by 2027/28 a cliff of £440k requires immediate action
findings.figures: £440k one-off grant in 2026/27; lost in 2027/28
findings.quote: the Council will need to plan for the loss of the Adjustment Support Grant in 2027/28 of £440k

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Loss of £832k of transitional protection funding over three years as government reforms local government finance
findings.detail: The Government's Fair Funding Review is phasing out transitional protection grants that have been supporting councils. Babergh will lose £146k in 2026/27, £273k in 2027/28, and £412k in 2028/29. This is separate from the main MTFP gap and represents a known cliff in funding that requires budget adjustment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that £832k of revenue is being withdrawn as government policy, not due to council underperformance; this is ringfenced budget pressure that must be solved through cuts or income
findings.quote: Transitional Protection Grant has been totally removed. This is a loss of £146k in 2026/27, £273k in 2027/28 and £412k in 2028/29. Total loss of £832k over the three years.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Unresolved budget gap of £9.656m over the five-year MTFP period, even after maximum permissible council tax rises
findings.detail: Over 2026/27 to 2030/31, the council faces a funding gap of £9.656m that has no identified solution. This gap persists after assuming the council will increase council tax by the maximum permitted under referendum rules each year. The council will need to identify £9.656m of additional savings or income but has not set out a plan for closing this gap.
findings.matters: This gap will force service reductions, further asset sales, or deterioration of service quality; the longer it remains unaddressed, the more severe the reductions required
findings.figures: £9.656m forecast gap over MTFP period (2026/27 to 2030/31) after assumed maximum council tax increases
findings.quote: there is a forecast budget gap over the MTFP period (2026/27 to 2030/31), (after assumed maximum increases in Council Tax), of £9.656m

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Babergh Growth Limited subsidiary will default on £3m of loan repayments to the council
findings.detail: The council's wholly-owned property company (Babergh Growth Limited) is unable to repay the full amount of principal and interest on loans made by the council. The shortfall is forecast at £3m, arising from a housing development at the former council offices in Hadleigh that has not performed as expected. The council must now charge this loss to its revenue budget as MRP.
findings.matters: A lender to the council is exposed to this loss; it consumes revenue that could service external debt and it demonstrates that property development risk taken by the council has crystallised, potentially signalling other capital schemes may also be at risk
findings.figures: £3m shortfall; £45k MRP charge in 2025/26, £47k in 2026/27 (over 30-year amortisation)
findings.quote: it is anticipated that the Council's subsidiary company, Babergh Growth Limited, will be unable to repay all of the loan (and interest) lent by the Council. The shortfall in the loan repayments is forecast at £3m

findings.paper_title: BC/25/37 2026-27 GF Final Budget Report
findings.headline: Medium-term reserves will be exhausted by 2029/30 if current trends continue
findings.detail: The council's MTFP remains unviable despite the 2026/27 improvement. The Financial Resilience Risk Reserve is projected to run out in 2029/30 under current assumptions. This is not a next-year problem but represents a structural funding gap that the council has acknowledged but not resolved.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion within 3-4 years signals the council cannot sustain services or meet obligations without material intervention — either drastic service cuts, significant tax increases, or access to capital markets being constrained
findings.figures: MTFP unviable; Financial Risk and Resilience Reserve runs out in 2029/30
findings.quote: the MTFP remains unviable with the Financial Risk and Resilience Reserve running out in 2029/30

findings.paper_title: BC/25/39 Capital Investment & Treasury Strategies 2026-27
findings.headline: Contingent property investment write-down risk: Babergh and Mid Suffolk have committed to report to Full Council if property valuations fall below purchase cost.
findings.detail: The Investment Strategy states that if valuations of directly-owned service investment property fall materially below purchase cost during the 2025/26 accounts, an updated strategy will be presented to Full Council detailing the impact on security and revenue consequences. This is a forward-looking acknowledgment that losses are possible.
findings.matters: Property investments secured the councils' loans to CIFCO Ltd and Gateway 14. A material fall in property values would reduce the security of those loans and could trigger additional provisions or write-downs against council finances.
findings.figures: No figures yet; contingent on 2025/26 Statement of Accounts revaluation
findings.quote: If during the preparation of the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts the value of these properties are materially below their purchase cost, then an updated investment strategy will be presented to Full Council detailing the impact of the loss on the security of investments and any revenue consequences.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/39 Capital Investment & Treasury Strategies 2026-27
findings.headline: Both councils face material governance risk from devolution: they assume they are 'going concerns' only until March 2028.
findings.detail: The Government's Devolution White Paper signals intention to replace the two-tier council structure with unitary councils and mayoral strategic authorities. The strategies are prepared on the assumption that Babergh and Mid Suffolk will continue to exist as going concerns 'until at least March 2028', explicitly acknowledging this is a contingent risk that is not yet resolved.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty about the borrower's continued existence. Any borrowing made now may be repaid by a different entity with different financial standing or not at all if councils merge or cease to exist.
findings.figures: March 2028 noted as the planning horizon beyond which continuity is uncertain
findings.quote: Through the English Devolution White Paper, the Government has signalled its intention to change how Local Government operates, replacing the two-tier council structure with new unitary councils and creating mayoral strategic authorities. This paper is prepared on the basis that the Councils will be going concerns, until at least March 2028.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/39 Capital Investment & Treasury Strategies 2026-27
findings.headline: Babergh's gross financing costs are forecast to rise to 37% of net revenue stream by 2029/30, approaching unsustainability.
findings.detail: Financing costs (interest and MRP) are growing as a share of the money available to run services. Starting at 26% in 2024/25, this rises to 37% by 2029/30, leaving only 63% of revenue for service delivery. The liability benchmark shows the council will be a long-term borrower with structural deficits driven by reduced government funding and lower growth in business rates.
findings.matters: When financing costs consume more than a third of net revenue, there is little flexibility to absorb budget pressures or invest in services. This metric is a leading indicator of councils in difficulty.
findings.figures: Babergh General Fund financing costs as % of net revenue: 26% (2024/25), 30% (2026/27), 37% (2029/30)
findings.quote: The results in Babergh indicate the reduction of Babergh's general fund reserves with the pressure to balance the budget

findings.paper_title: BC/25/39 Capital Investment & Treasury Strategies 2026-27
findings.headline: Babergh's usable reserves are forecast to fall by more than half, from £50.7m to £24.4m, over the five-year plan.
findings.detail: The document notes that this decline is driven by pressure to balance the budget and use of reserves to fund the capital programme in the HRA. The council cannot adopt Mid Suffolk's strategy of funding capital from reserves to avoid borrowing, specifically because it lacks sufficient reserves.
findings.matters: Falling reserves are a key indicator of financial stress. A council losing half its reserves over five years signals deteriorating financial sustainability and reduced headroom to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: Babergh usable reserves: 2024/25 actual £50.7m, declining to £24.4m by 2030/31
findings.quote: The results in Babergh indicate the reduction of Babergh's general fund reserves with the pressure to balance the budget and the use of reserves to fund the capital programme in the HRA.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/38 2026-27 HRA Final budget report
findings.headline: Capital investment of £16.9m funded by a mix of shrinking Right to Buy receipts, declining reserves, and increased reliance on revenue drawdown
findings.detail: Capital programme funded from: RTB receipts (£3.044m), Major Repairs Reserve (£4.232m, the depreciation charge), Revenue Contribution to Capital (£9.126m drawn from operating reserves), and external grant. RTB receipt funding is volatile: 24 completions in first half 2025/26 despite budgeting for 6, but new lower discounts expected to reduce volumes sharply. The council is increasing reliance on revenue contribution from depleting reserves.
findings.matters: As RTB receipts become less reliable and reserves deplete, the council is using more of its limited operating surplus for capital, leaving even less for day-to-day operations. This is unsustainable beyond the current reserve balance.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital budget £16.934m; RTB receipts £3.044m; Revenue Contribution to Capital £9.126m; maximum RTB discount reduced from £136k to £16-34k
findings.quote: Following the 2024 Autumn Statement, in which the Government announced a significant reduction in Right to Buy (RTB) discounts...this spike is expected to be temporary, with volumes forecast to fall sharply next year.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/38 2026-27 HRA Final budget report
findings.headline: Regulatory and compliance costs driving significant new budget pressures: damp, mould, Awaab's Law, Decent Homes Standard 2, carbon neutrality
findings.detail: The budget includes £150k for damp and mould surveys (new for 2026/27), £150k for disrepair costs, £95k for asbestos work, plus ongoing costs for Health and Safety compliance and building regulations post-Grenfell. New legislation (Social Housing Regulation Act 2023, Decent Homes Standard 2) is expected to drive further costs. Pension contribution reductions of £281k are a one-off gain being overwhelmed by compliance spending.
findings.matters: These are non-discretionary costs driven by regulation and resident safety. They cannot be cut without regulatory breach. The trend is increasing, not decreasing. Capital programme includes £2.895m for Social Housing Decarbonisation (matched funding) indicating external grant dependency to meet decarbonisation deadlines.
findings.figures: £150k damp/mould surveys (new); £150k disrepair; £95k asbestos; £2.895m capital decarbonisation match fund
findings.quote: Increased buildings compliance and regulatory requirements, particularly post Grenfell and including new targets for carbon neutrality.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/38 2026-27 HRA Final budget report
findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges HRA financial challenges are structural and sector-wide, dating back to 2002 policy decisions
findings.detail: The report traces the problem to formula rent (2002), followed by 1% rent reductions (2016-2020), then a 7% cap in 2023/24. These government policies created a financial position that the council cannot solve with local management alone. The majority of councils are in the same situation and lobbying central government.
findings.matters: This signals that Babergh's HRA problems are not a local management failure but a national policy issue. No amount of operational efficiency will fix this. Lending decisions need to account for the fact that future government policy choices (on rent caps, regulation, capital support) will determine the HRA's financial outcome more than management action.
findings.figures: Five years of 1% annual rent reductions (2016-2020); 7% cap applied in 2023/24 against 10.1% CPI
findings.quote: It is important to note that the reasons for the challenges around the HRA account are complex and date back to 2002. The majority of Councils are in a similar position, and the sector continues to lobby Central Government.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/38 2026-27 HRA Final budget report
findings.headline: Annual HRA deficits of £8.8m+ sustained by drawing down reserves, not a balanced operating position
findings.detail: 2026/27 deficit of £8.855m (up from £8.353m in 2025/26) will be funded entirely from reserves. This is structural: operating income (rents, service charges) does not cover operating and capital costs. Even with a 4.8% rent rise, the council still runs a deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that this is not a temporary position. The council is living off reserves accumulated decades ago. At this depletion rate, the HRA will become insolvent within 5-10 years unless either deficits close dramatically or external funding is secured.
findings.figures: 2026/27 deficit £8.855m; 2025/26 budget deficit £8.353m; £502k increase year-on-year
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget was a deficit of £8.353m, the budget position for 2026/27 is a deficit of £8.855m, an increase of £502k.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/38 2026-27 HRA Final budget report
findings.headline: Strategic reserves declining to £3.2m by March 2027, eroding the buffer available for pressures
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves forecast to fall from £14.856m (March 2025) to £12.079m (March 2026) to £3.224m (March 2027). The working balance stays at only £1m (under £300 per property). With annual deficits of £8.8m, reserves are being depleted rapidly.
findings.matters: Reserves are the only buffer against unforeseen costs (regulatory changes, void spikes, compliance failures). Declining to £3.2m represents minimal headroom for a 3,555-dwelling stock facing significant compliance and maintenance demands.
findings.figures: Strategic reserves £14.856m (March 2025) → £12.079m (March 2026) → £3.224m (March 2027); working balance £1m
findings.quote: The total balance of all earmarked reserves at 31 March 2027, as a result of the budget proposals, is forecast to be £4.224m, which equates to £1,188 per property.

findings.paper_title: BC/25/38 2026-27 HRA Final budget report
findings.headline: Business plan sustainability depends entirely on government rent convergence decision that was only confirmed 28 January 2026
findings.detail: The 30-year business plan assumes £1/week rent convergence in 2027/28 and £2/week thereafter. If not implemented, this costs £6.28m in lost rental income over 30 years. The decision was delayed from the Autumn Statement and only confirmed weeks before this budget was set. Future viability is contingent on government continuing to allow these increases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's stated 30-year financial sustainability is a policy choice by central government rather than a structural solution. Rent increases can be reversed or capped again at any time.
findings.figures: £6.28m loss over 30 years if convergence not implemented; £1 in 2027/28, £2 per week from 2028/29
findings.quote: If this is not implemented the effect will be a loss of £6.28m rental income over the 30 years of the business plan.

findings.paper_title: JASC Capital Investment Treasury Strategy Issued to JASC
findings.headline: Councils' financial plans are conditional on no local government restructuring before March 2028
findings.detail: The strategy paper states explicitly that the councils' plans are based on them being 'going concerns until at least March 2028'. However, the Government's Devolution White Paper has signalled intention to replace the current two-tier council structure with unitary councils and mayoral authorities. This means the medium-term financial assumptions may be rendered moot by structural reform within 2-3 years.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of structural certainty. If councils are due to be reconfigured or abolished within the MTFP period, the multi-year financial forecasts and borrowing commitments become less reliable and execution risk increases significantly.
findings.figures: March 2028 is the assumed end date for current council structures
findings.quote: This paper is prepared on the basis that the Councils will be going concerns, until at least March 2028. It is important, however, to note the impact devolution and local government reform will have.

findings.paper_title: JASC Capital Investment Treasury Strategy Issued to JASC
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk's strategy to fund the capital programme from reserves will deplete reserves by £29m in one year (2025/26 to 2026/27)
findings.detail: Mid Suffolk is choosing to fund General Fund capital from reserves instead of borrowing, which reduces future MRP charges but accelerates reserve depletion. Usable reserves are forecast to drop from £111.5m to £82.3m in 2026/27 alone—a single-year reduction of 26%. The council is deliberately trading financial resilience for lower future debt charges.
findings.matters: While this approach reduces borrowing need, it materially weakens the council's financial buffer. A lender would want to understand the minimum reserve threshold and whether this strategy is sustainable given the scale of annual drawdowns.
findings.figures: Usable reserves drop from £111.5m (2025/26 forecast) to £82.3m (2026/27), a £29m reduction in one year, declining further to £74.6m by 2030/31
findings.quote: For the 2026/27 budget and MTFP period the strategy in the General Fund for Mid Suffolk is to fund the capital programme from reserves instead of borrowing to reduce the need to provide MRP.

findings.paper_title: JASC Capital Investment Treasury Strategy Issued to JASC
findings.headline: Government funding for 2026/27 onwards remains undefined and unbudgeted pending the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement
findings.detail: The strategy document explicitly states that no government grants have been assumed for the 2026/27 budget or the MTFP period. This means the financial forecasts for both councils are contingent on an announcement that has not yet been received. For Babergh, with its tight budget position, this is a material uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that revenue forecasts and debt service capability are based on known income. Unbudgeted government support creates uncertainty and suggests the financial plans may need material revision once the settlement is known.
findings.figures: No government grants assumed for General Fund from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: For the draft budget and MTFP no Government grants have been currently assumed subject to receiving the Provisional Local Government Finance settlement.

findings.paper_title: JASC Capital Investment Treasury Strategy Issued to JASC
findings.headline: Babergh's usable reserves are declining by 36% over five years, from £47.6m to £30.6m
findings.detail: Babergh's general fund reserves are forecast to decline from £47.6m in 2025/26 to £30.6m by 2030/31, a reduction of £17m. The paper explicitly attributes this to pressure to balance the budget and using reserves to fund HRA capital expenditure. This reduces the council's financial resilience and buffer for managing unexpected pressures or interest rate rises.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce a council's ability to absorb financial shocks or manage temporary deficits. Combined with Babergh's rising financing costs and the Babergh Growth loss, this indicates tightening financial headroom.
findings.figures: Usable reserves declining from £47.6m to £30.6m, a reduction of £17m or 36% over five years
findings.quote: The results in Babergh indicate the reduction of Babergh's general fund reserves with the pressure to balance the budget and the use of reserves to fund the capital programme in the HRA.

findings.paper_title: JASC Capital Investment Treasury Strategy Issued to JASC
findings.headline: Babergh's financing costs will reach 43% of net revenue stream by 2029/30, leaving minimal budget flexibility
findings.detail: The proportion of gross financing costs (interest payable on borrowing and MRP charges) to net revenue stream for Babergh peaks at 43% in 2029/30 in the General Fund. This compares to Mid Suffolk at only 18% for the same year. This means Babergh has committed 43 pence of every pound of revenue to servicing debt, with the trend worsening from 37% in 2026/27 to 43%.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand debt sustainability and headroom for service provision or responding to financial shocks. A financing cost ratio of 43% is extremely high and indicates Babergh has little flexibility if revenue falls or rates rise further.
findings.figures: Babergh 43% by 2029/30 (rising from 37% in 2026/27), compared to Mid Suffolk 18%
findings.quote: Table 4 shows the maximum level of financing costs to net revenue stream for Babergh is 43% and for Mid Suffolk is 1 8% for the  General Fund.

findings.paper_title: JASC Capital Investment Treasury Strategy Issued to JASC
findings.headline: Babergh Growth Ltd has a £3m expected credit loss and will not repay its £13.7m loan to the council
findings.detail: Babergh council lent £13.7m to a joint venture company (Babergh Growth Ltd) to develop housing at the former council offices in Hadleigh. Due to increased costs and lower than expected returns, the company is not expected to repay the loan. Discussions with auditors are ongoing about recognising a £3m expected credit loss, of which only £938k is currently reserved, leaving a £2m gap.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the council has an unrecovered investment of this scale and an unresolved loss provision that may impact future financial statements and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £13.7m loan, £3m expected credit loss, £938k reserve in place, gap of approximately £2m
findings.quote: As a result of increased costs and lower than expected returns Babergh Growth is not expected to repay the loan. No future schemes are planned for Babergh Growth Ltd.
